title: Bounds & error intervals
examples: When we round a number, how do we find the possible range for the actual value?
If I calculate something using rounded measurements, how do I find the biggest and smallest possible answer?
What is the difference between truncation and rounding when finding bounds?

explain.say: Today we learn about error intervals. These help us find a range for an answer. We use this when measurements are not exact.

draw.text: Error Intervals: Range of possible values

explain.say: First we look at upper and lower bounds. These are the maximum and minimum possible values. If a measurement is three point two metres, the lower bound is three point one five. The upper bound is three point two five.

Next we look at truncation. This means cutting off digits. If we truncate to two decimal places, the lower bound is the number itself. The upper bound is one less than the next place value. For three point two, the upper bound is three point two four nine nine... effectively three point two five.

items: Upper bound: One less than next place value

explain.say: Finally we use bounds in calculations. To find the maximum possible value, we use the upper bounds for all measurements. To find the minimum, we use the lower bounds for all measurements.

draw.text: Max = Upper bounds, Min = Lower bounds

faq.q: What is the difference between truncation and rounding?
faq.a: Truncation means simply cutting off the digits after a certain point. Rounding means adjusting the last kept digit based on the next digit. You might also hear this called 'cutting off' or 'nearest value'.
asks: How do I truncate a number?
Is truncation the same as rounding down?

faq.q: Do I always use the upper bound for the maximum value?
faq.a: Yes, for most simple calculations, you use the upper bound for every measurement. This gives you the largest possible result. You could also ask this as 'What gives the biggest answer?'
asks: Should I use the upper bound for maximum?
How do I get the largest possible result?

faq.q: If I have two measurements, how do I find the smallest possible area?
faq.a: To find the smallest area, you must use the lower bound for both the length and the width. You multiply the two lower bounds together. You could also ask this as 'Minimum area calculation' or 'Smallest possible area'.

faq.q: Does the number of significant figures matter?
faq.a: Yes, the number of significant figures tells you the precision of the measurement. This determines how many places you must use for your upper and lower bounds. You could also ask this as 'How many digits to use?'

faq.q: What if one measurement is given as an exact integer?
faq.a: If a measurement is given as an exact integer, you treat it as having zero error. You use that number as both the upper and lower bound. You could also ask this as 'No error measurement' or 'Exact value'.

facts: The lower bound is always less than or equal to the actual value.
The upper bound is always greater than or equal to the actual value.
When calculating a product, the maximum result uses all upper bounds.
When calculating a product, the minimum result uses all lower bounds.

quiz.say: A length is measured as 12 point 5 cm, accurate to the nearest centimetre. What is the lower bound?
quiz.why: Since it is accurate to the nearest centimetre, the lower bound is one centimetre less than the stated value.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because it rounds up instead of finding the minimum possible value.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake because students forget to subtract one full unit.
wrong.3: This assumes the measurement is exact, ignoring the stated accuracy.

quiz.say: A rectangle has a width of 5 point 2 metres and a length of 3 point 1 metres. What is the maximum possible area?
quiz.why: To find the maximum area, you multiply the upper bound of the width by the upper bound of the length.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it uses the stated measurements without accounting for the error range.
wrong.2: This mistake occurs when students incorrectly subtract the lower bounds.
wrong.3: This happens if students add the two measurements together instead of multiplying.

quiz.say: If a time is measured as 45 seconds, accurate to the nearest five seconds, what is the upper bound?
quiz.why: Since it is accurate to the nearest five seconds, the upper bound is five seconds more than the stated value.

wrong.0: This suggests a decimal error when the accuracy is given in whole five-second steps.
wrong.1: This is technically correct but the question implies the interval boundary, not the upper bound itself.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates the lower bound instead of the upper bound.
